Every month I get a lot of reports, and I read very few of them all the way through. So let me tell you what I actually do with a forty-page budget report. I go to page one and I look for one figure, the total, and I ask how much of it is already spent. Then I go to the breakdown, and I am not looking for the big lines. The big lines never surprise anybody. I am looking for the small lines that doubled. A line that goes from a little to roughly twice as much in one quarter is a story, and somebody should be able to tell it to me in two sentences. Then I look at the trend over twelve months, never one month on its own, because one month is a peak or a dip and it does not mean anything yet. That takes me about four minutes. I do not need many numbers. I need a few numbers and the story behind them.

Here is the mistake I see most often when people present data. They show too many numbers. Twelve figures on one slide, every one of them correct, and nobody in the room can remember any of them five minutes later. The fix is not to have less data. You should have a lot of data. The fix is to show a few numbers and say what they mean. Instead of saying our average cost per visit is three hundred and twelve reais, say the average visit costs roughly three hundred reais, and that is twice what we planned. Round the number, then compare it to something. A percentage on its own is not a story. Nineteen percent means nothing until you say nineteen against a target of twenty-two. And one more thing. When there is not much good news, do not hide it in the middle of the slide. Put it first, say it in one sentence, and then show how much budget you need to fix it.

Researchers asked people to remember numbers from a short business presentation, and the results were surprising. When the presenter showed more than five figures, people remembered almost none of them. When the presenter showed only three, and connected each one to a comparison, most people remembered all three a week later. The comparison was the key. Two million liters means very little to most people. Two million liters, double what we sold last year, means a lot. The same researchers found that rounded numbers felt more honest, not less. People trusted roughly twenty percent more than nineteen point seven percent, because the rounded number sounded like somebody who understood the data rather than somebody reading it from a screen.
